text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in Russian newspapers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
SEVODNYA
- Ban on street sale of spirits in Russia is likely to lead to a significant rise in retail prices for these products.
- Spanish King Juan Carlos has much to teach the Russian authorities about political concord and reconciliation.
- Deputy director of the Federal Bankruptcy Administration Pyotr Karpov, recently arrested on corruption allegations, is said to know a lot about budget debtors.
- In response to the Finance Ministry sequester proposals, the State Duma is preparing a bill on monetary emission.
- First Deputy Prime Minister Boris Nemtsov is to take special care of the state-run oil company Rosneft.
KOMMERSANT DAILY
- The State Duma lower house of the Russian parliament is not likely to approve the government's sequester plan.

- Due to serious differences in economic and financial policies of Russia and Belarus, unification of the two countries would require additional efforts in these spheres, says Alexander Livshits, deputy head of President Yeltsin's administration.
- President Yeltsin turned down two bills that could have improved the position of taxpayers.
- Russia's Central Bank proposed that the rouble become a reserve currency for the Commonwealth of Independent States, but other CIS national banks are not likely to agree to it.
- Conflict between First Deputy Prime Minister Boris Nemtsov and Rem Vyakhirev, the head of gas giant Gazprom, seems to be over.
- Convertible bonds of the Russian oil company Lukoil are to start circulating on London Stock Exchange.
NEZAVISIMAYA GAZETA
- Boris Nemtsov has initiated an oil and gas revolution in Russia, which may lead to losing the country's monopoly on its domestic fuel market.
- According to Boris Yeltsin's decision, the country's Security Council is the only coordinating body in settlement of the Chechen crisis.
ROSSIISKIYE VESTI
- Not only communist opposition but some democratic polititians and economists in Russia tend to blame the International Monetary Fund for the country's economic problems.
PRAVDA-5
- The state-run oil company Rosneft is a very tempting prey for the Russian financial and political oligarchy.
-- Svetlana Kovaleva, Moscow Newsroom, +7095 941 8520
